The North Sea ecosystem has been struggling to maintain its balance due to anthropogenic pressures such as overfishing and pollution. As part of the Biodiversity Strategy (also subject of the EU's Green Deal) Member States have committed to achieving additional protection and improved ecological robustness of a transboundary network of marine protected areas (MPAs). It has been agreed that by 2030 a total of 30% of Europe's seas will be protected, 10% of which is strictly protected, so additional nature protection areas will be added. The definition of nature-protection areas and translation to legally binding nature restoration targets and what this means in practice for space reservation is currently work in progress for most member states, following the EU nature protection objectives. Natura2000 is the current network of breeding and resting sites for rare and threatened species and rare natural habitat types which are protected. They can be found across all EU countries, both on land and at sea. The aim of the network is to ensure long-term survival of Europe's most valuable and threatened species and habitats, listed under both the [Birds and Habitats Directive](https://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/natura2000/index_en.htm). Natura2000 and (future) MPAs pose constraints to other uses in that area. These uses may not disturb the protected species in the given area. For example, wind farms are not allowed to be built inside nature-protection areas and sand mining activities are not permitted.
